about: Per later attempt: what the later team did, then what they found. Written by a model from that attempt's own sources only (the later paper's abstract, the authors' own words, a reviewer's note; the original study only for comparison), refused by a mechanical check if it named a number, name or qualifier its sources lack, then checked against those sources by a second model (claude-haiku-5-5, verify_v1). Every passage that check flagged was read against its sources by Claude (an AI model, not the writer) and edited, accepted or held back; a random sample of 100 passages it passed was also read in full. `read_on` is set when Claude read the passage itself; `edited` records any change the reader made; `sample_read` marks the sampled passages. Producer: /root/wiki-scratch/pilot_v3.py; decisions: /root/wiki-scratch/verify_reading.py; importer: /root/wiki-scratch/import_verified.py. Re-analyses (reproductions) were written with the re-analysis wording of the same instructions (/root/wiki-scratch/pilot_v4r.py) and every one was read against its sources by Claude (importer: /root/wiki-scratch/import_repro.py).

at_000831535b.did: In a conceptual replication, participants solved linear systems of equations problems. Each was shown the problem as a single representation (a graphic, a text, or a formula), or as a combination: text with graphic (heterogeneous) or text with formula (homogeneous). The team also tracked where people looked.
at_000831535b.found: Performance was superior with combinations of representations than with a single one, in accordance with the original finding. Text with a graphic saved time compared with text with a formula, which raised the mental effort needed (cognitive load). Contrary to previous research, people looked at the text least, and the graphic helped most.

at_0120fbd149.did: Young adults (18-23 years) and older adults (52-56 years) rated words for the age they learned them and for how familiar they were. Both groups then did a lexical decision task (deciding quickly whether letters form a real word), and a task sorting words into artifact or naturally occurring categories.
at_0120fbd149.found: The age-of-acquisition and familiarity ratings differed significantly between young and older adults. In both tasks, the effects of age of acquisition and familiarity also differed significantly between the two groups. The authors say the results fit the idea that age-of-acquisition effects cannot be accounted for by word frequency or other possible confounds.

at_015bdcdace.did: The team re-tested the earlier idea that losing a job changes personality. They compared how people's scores on the five broad personality traits psychologists usually measure (the Big Five) changed over time between those who lost their jobs and those who did not. They also checked whether the length of unemployment or gender made a difference.
at_015bdcdace.found: Job loss had no effect on any of the five traits, and unemployment duration and gender made no difference either. Analyses accounting for possible selection effects gave comparable results. This does not match the original finding of personality change after unemployment.

at_08a3142283.did: In a preregistered retest, 36 new participants judged where things were, using sounds alone, visual signals alone, and the two together. The team compared how precise people were with both signals against what maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), a formula that weights each sense by its reliability, predicts.
at_08a3142283.found: Participants reduced their variability with both signals in line with MLE. But they weighed the visual signals significantly stronger than MLE predicts. The authors conclude observers did not weight audiovisual spatial signals exactly in proportion to their reliabilities, unlike the original's near-optimal result. They call these deviations small and suggest they may come from people's uncertainty about whether the sound and the light came from the same event.

at_0b696af6ce.did: Children aged 3 years to 4 years 7 months were tested on arrays of objects. They were asked about adding objects to an array, whether two arrays had the same number, and which array had more. They were also asked about equality and inequality when the objects were misaligned or spatially transformed.
at_0b696af6ce.found: The children answered correctly when objects were added, when arrays were numerically equal, and when comparing relative numbers. The earlier claim that very young children understand that a number of objects stays the same when the objects are moved, with a decline and rise in performance, was not confirmed.

at_0cbeaadd60.did: In a replication with procedures very similar to the original and a sample more than 5 times larger, a total of 260 people held either a hand warmer or a cold pack for 1 minute. at_0cbeaadd60.found: People who held the cold pack did not report being lonelier than people who held the warm pack, and the effect size was essentially zero. The effect also stayed nonsignificant after excluding people who reported suspicion about the link between the warmth-coldness manipulation and the loneliness measure. at_b51c8da5a4.did: In 19 geopolitical regions, 4,724 participants read vignettes about a person who believed something. Some stories were standard cases where the belief was justified and true. at_b51c8da5a4.found: Participants were 1.86 times more likely to say the person knew in standard cases than in Gettier-type cases. The original study found knowledge attributed in Gettier-type cases at rates similar to standard cases, so this result was not the same. The size of the gap varied by story, and the original study's story produced the smallest gap. The authors say the results suggest Gettier intuitions may be common across different scenarios and cultural contexts, and that lay people may rely on a shared set of epistemic intuitions (a core folk epistemology) that requires more than justification, belief and truth. They add that epistemic intuitions may also depend on contextual factors unrelated to the criteria of knowledge, such as the characteristics of the protagonist.

at_f0420db483.found: Pupil dilation depended on how quickly the solution came. at_fa68673afc.did: Across three laboratory experiments and one field experiment (241, 465, 201 and 74 people), participants were primed with a goal for effective performance or ineffective performance (the later two laboratory experiments added a neutral prime). The field experiment used employees in a customer service department of a large communication company.
at_fa68673afc.found: The hypothesis that feedback amplifies the effect of a primed goal on performance was supported. In the first experiment, the primed goal for effective performance led to higher performance than the primed goal for ineffective performance. Feedback, regardless of its sign, increased task and creative performance when the primed goal was for effective performance, but not when it was for ineffective performance. This was replicated in the two later laboratory experiments, which had three primed goal conditions (effective, neutral, ineffective). In experiments 2 and 3, a goal that participants set consciously, without being prompted, mediated the relationship between the primed goal and performance when feedback was given. The field experiment, in a work setting, was a conceptual replication. A meta-analysis of the four experiments found an average effect whose range of plausible values excluded zero, with no evidence of heterogeneity across them. The authors suggest that subconscious goals are a foundation for the difficulty level of consciously set goals, and that subconscious and conscious goals work together in affecting performance.

at_1becf88f4d.did: The team re-analysed choice data from two earlier studies that used convex time budgets, a method where people split money or effort between a sooner and a later date. at_2f704f13fb.did: Participants pressed a left or right key as soon as they detected a light moving at 2 degrees per second. at_2f704f13fb.found: Both experiments showed strong compatibility effects of position and direction of motion on responses. A Simon effect, where an irrelevant position still influenced the response, appeared only in the first experiment when position was task irrelevant. The selective lack of a Simon effect supports the integrated model of Umiltà and Nicoletti (1992), in which the Simon effect requires orienting of attention triggered by the saccade program but not by the pursuit program.

at_2fe96fd61b.did: In Experiments 1 and 2, people did a task where the location of a stimulus told them which response to make, with a mapping that was incompatible. In some conditions of Experiments 1-3, the mode of presentation differed between the two kinds of trials.
at_2fe96fd61b.found: Experiments 1 and 2 showed a reverse Simon effect: on location-irrelevant trials, responses were faster when stimulus and response locations did not correspond than when they did. Experiment 4 showed that differences in physical characteristics between the two kinds of stimuli were not enough to remove the reverse Simon effect. The authors conclude that the short-term associations between stimulus location information and responses are relatively mode specific.

at_610498d887.did: Twenty-four participants answered questions using only a tree diagram or a 2×2 table, with no added text. at_62343a9b44.did: Eighty-five undergraduates filled in self-report questionnaires and did a working memory task in which they handled words (the operation span, OSPAN). On Day 1 they incidentally encoded negative and neutral items together with context information. On Day 2 they were given an unexpected memory test.
at_62343a9b44.found: Negative items brought more hits and more false alarms on item memory, and lower accuracy on context memory, than neutral items, replicating previous findings. Under low working memory capacity, high anxiety sensitivity and looming cognitive style predicted high dissociation and low accuracy for negative item memory. The authors suggest dissociation could be a coping strategy for reducing negative item memory, with working memory capacity buffering against these vulnerabilities. The sample was nonclinical, which limits generalizing the results to clinical samples.

at_6781bb007b.did: TgF344-AD rats, which develop amyloid plaques, had one side of the brain exposed to low-dose radiation (2 Gray a day for 5 days) at 9 months or at 19 months old. at_6781bb007b.found: At the early stage, TSPO levels, a marker of neuroinflammation, normalized across the brain. at_da6e370f1d.did: In a series of studies, people worked on the classic Linda conjunction problem. The team looked at what meanings people gave to the word 'probability', designed contexts that pointed to its mathematical meanings, and compared this with questions worded as 'frequency'.
at_da6e370f1d.found: People read 'probability' in the Linda problem in nonmathematical ways. at_eb476915ae.found: Responses were slower for negative cues followed by negative targets than by positive targets, and faster for positive cues followed by positive than by negative targets, matching Chao's findings. at_2b285947e3.did: The study compared the effects of beliefs about absolute ability and about ability relative to others on satisfaction with a performance, self-evaluations and bets on future performance. In the first experiment, undergraduates were told they had answered 20% or 80% correct on a practice test, or received no score. Separately, they were told they placed in the 23rd or 77th percentile, or received no comparative feedback. They then bet on two games: one needing more than 50% right to double their money, and one needing to beat more than 50% of other test-takers.
at_2b285947e3.found: Absolute feedback influenced comparative betting, particularly when no comparative feedback was available, while comparative feedback exerted weaker and inconsistent effects on absolute bets. Absolute feedback also had stronger and more consistent effects on satisfaction with performance and on state self-esteem. A second experiment in a different university sample replicated these effects, and showed that they emerge even when bets are placed after satisfaction is rated. The authors suggest that information about one's absolute standing may be more influential than information about comparative standing, partially supporting a key tenet of Festinger's (1954) social comparison theory.

at_d4d76657cd.did: 574 online workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) were given made-up performance feedback on a word-puzzle (anagram) test, relative to two potential matching partners in a sham chat room, so that the comparison with the partner was favorable or unfavorable (temporal social comparison, varied within each person). In a high-competition condition they could earn an extra $1.00 by outperforming their partner; in a low-competition condition they could earn it by passing a threshold unrelated to the partner. Their preference for being matched with each partner was recorded, as the measure of social undermining (unwillingness to be matched).
at_d4d76657cd.found: Competition and the comparison feedback interacted. In the high-competition condition, participants showed a significantly higher preference for being matched with the partner with the favorable comparison than with the partner with the unfavorable one. In the low-competition condition, there was no significant difference. The authors report this as the same pattern as the original, a successful replication by the project's criteria, so a second stage of data collection was not needed.

at_d8bf3464ea.did: In the later study, run online in Italian rather than English, 477 adults aged 18 to 64 filled in personality questions about openness to experience and a task in which they named animals. at_dc556122d9.did: The team did not collect new data. at_dc556122d9.found: Self-regulation was positively and statistically significantly associated with GPA, while the self-discipline trait was not associated with GPA over and above self-regulation. at_de52053b03.did: In a replication of Study 5b of the original paper, 533 adults from ten age groups between 18 and 69 rated how kind, honest, nice and good people were at five points in time: today, around the year the participant turned 20, the year they were born, 20 years before they were born, and 40 years before they were born. The team compared the average ratings at neighbouring time points.
at_de52053b03.found: Ratings were lower for today than for the time when participants were 20, and lower for that time than for their birth year. Ratings for the birth year and 20 years before birth were equivalent, and so were ratings for 20 years before birth and 40 years before birth. So, as in the original, participants perceived moral decline during their own lifetime but not for the periods before they were born. The authors report that all primary findings replicated, with the same pattern as the original; the only minor difference was that the original could not show the last two time points were equivalent, while this study did.

at_eab7befc87.did: The team ran three replications, with 653 participants in all, of studies on whether anchoring (the pull of numerical estimates toward a number considered earlier) from self-generated and from experimenter-provided anchors depends on other factors. at_eab7befc87.found: The team found no evidence that either type of anchoring was moderated by cognitive load, nor by need for cognition or forewarnings across the three replications, so the moderation reported in the original was not found again. at_fe0b236ee9.did: In a replication of the original paper's first experiment, 26 participants in the analysis sample (from 48 tested) tried to identify a single letter shown for different durations.
